Duryodhana lies on the ground and can't get up. The fight is over. The Pandavas have won the war. And for a moment, nobody behaves the way winners are supposed to. Bhima walks over to the fallen king and puts his foot on his head. Yudhishthira, his own brother, tells him to stop. And Balarama, the teacher who trained both fighters, is so angry at the blow he just saw that he lifts his plough, his own weapon, and runs at Bhima. The victory itself is put on trial.
screen: `THE KING CAN'T RISE.` → `A FOOT ON HIS HEAD.` → `THE TEACHER CHARGES.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's telling, Yudhishthira tells Bhima that this man is a king, and their kinsman, and that his foot does him no honor. Krishna catches hold of Balarama before he reaches Bhima, and reminds him of Bhima's vow from the dice hall and the wrongs done to the Pandavas. Balarama isn't persuaded. Bhima will be remembered as a crooked fighter, he says, in effect, and he leaves for Dvaraka in anger. The teacher of both men walks away from the winner. Then the fallen king speaks. Duryodhana, unable to stand, turns on Krishna and lists the deaths he calls unfair: Bhishma behind Shikhandi, Drona and the false news about his son, Karna with his wheel stuck in the earth. Krishna answers with a list of his own: the poison, the house of lac, the dice, Draupadi dragged into the hall. Your own wrongs brought you here, he says. Duryodhana answers that he lived as a king should, ruled, gave, fought, and now goes to heaven with his friends. Then the text does something strange. Flowers rain down from the sky on Duryodhana, music sounds, and the Pandavas stand there downcast. Krishna tells them plainly that these warriors could not have been killed in a fair fight, and that what was done was done for them. The epic doesn't settle the argument. It lets the winner, the loser and the teacher each speak, and lets the flowers fall where they fall.
screen: `YUDHISHTHIRA REBUKES BHIMA` · `BALARAMA LEAVES IN ANGER` · `TWO LISTS OF WRONGS` · then, large: `FLOWERS ON THE LOSER`

849.title: Sauptika: the night massacre
849.hook: three men are all that's left of an army, and a dying king makes one of them its commander
849.howItsDone: Sauptika, from a Sanskrit word for sleep, is the name of the tenth of the Mahabharata's eighteen books, and reciters of the whole epic carry the story straight on from the fallen king into the night raid.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Shalya book closed with Balarama's anger, two lists of wrongs, and flowers falling on the man who lost. Your line was let the flowers fall where they fall.

Evening on the battlefield. Three warriors come looking for their king: Ashvatthama, the son of Drona; Kripa, the old teacher of the princes; and Kritavarma, a fighter from Krishna's own clan who fought on the other side. They're the last of the Kaurava army still standing. They find Duryodhana where Bhima left him, his thighs broken, covered in dust, unable to rise. The man who once commanded a vast host now has three men and a darkening sky. This is Sauptika, the book of the night.
screen: `THREE WARRIORS LEFT.` → `THEY FIND THEIR KING.` → `THE BOOK OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's telling, the three weep at the sight of him. Duryodhana, in pain, still speaks like a king. Don't grieve, he tells them; he fought and didn't turn his back, and this is the way of the world. But Ashvatthama can't let it rest. His grief runs into something older. He remembers how his own father, Drona, died: told a lie about his son's death, laying down his weapons, and then killed. Now he sees his king broken by a blow below the waist. He makes a vow before Duryodhana, in effect: before this night is over, I'll send the Panchalas to the land of the dead. Then Duryodhana, who can't stand and has no army, asks Kripa to bring a pot of water. With that water, lying in the dust, he has Kripa install Ashvatthama as commander of the army. Of what army? Of three men. The ceremony is real to them anyway. Ashvatthama embraces the king, the three go off into the night, and Duryodhana is left alone on the field. A small scene, almost quiet, but everything in this book grows out of it: a vow made in grief, a title given by a man who has nothing left to give, and a commander with no one to lead but two companions and his own anger.

850.title: Sauptika: the night massacre
850.hook: two men sleep under a banyan tree, and the third lies awake watching an owl hunt

segments.voice: Yesterday: a dying king made Ashvatthama commander, with a pot of water, of an army of three. Your line was an army of three.

A huge banyan tree in a forest at night, its branches full of sleeping crows. Under it, three tired warriors have stopped to rest. They've ridden away from the field, afraid the Pandavas might find them. Kripa lies down and sleeps. Kritavarma sleeps too; they've been fighting for days. But Ashvatthama can't sleep. He lies on the ground with his eyes open, burning, the text says, with anger and grief. And up in the branches, something moves.
screen: `A BANYAN FULL OF CROWS.` → `TWO MEN SLEEP.` → `ONE LIES AWAKE.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's telling, an owl comes down through the dark, large and fierce, with sharp talons, and lands among the crows while they sleep. One by one, it kills them. The crows don't wake in time to fly. By the end, the ground under the tree is scattered with their bodies, and the owl sits there, pleased with its night's work. Ashvatthama watches the whole thing. And he says to himself, in effect: this owl has taught me something. The Pandavas can't be beaten in open battle. They've won; they're strong, and they have Krishna. But they'll be asleep tonight, tired and celebrating. I can do what the owl did. Notice what the epic is doing here. Nobody gives Ashvatthama the idea. No god speaks, no adviser plots. He finds it in a tree, at the hour when he should be resting, with his companions asleep beside him. A sleepless mind reads a lesson into whatever it sees. The owl only hunted. It was Ashvatthama who made it a plan. And because his companions are asleep, no one is awake to hear it said aloud. That's the hinge of the whole night: it starts as grief and anger, and under the banyan, it becomes a method.
screen: `THE OWL AMONG THE CROWS` · `THE CROWS NEVER WAKE` · `"THE OWL HAS TAUGHT ME"` · then, large: `GRIEF BECOMES A PLAN`

851.title: Sauptika: the night massacre
851.hook: an old teacher is shaken awake in the dark and told the plan, and he tries to talk his nephew out of it
851.carry: two good arguments losing to one sleepless man
851.howItsDone: Kripa's counsel under the banyan, with its talk of fate and human effort working together, is a passage some readers return to when they think about fate and action in the Mahabharata.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ashvatthama lay awake under the banyan and watched an owl kill the sleeping crows. Your line was the owl only hunted.

Kripa opens his eyes. It's still dark. His nephew is standing over him, and so is Kritavarma, who's been woken too. Ashvatthama tells them what he saw in the tree and what he means to do: go to the Pandava camp tonight, while everyone sleeps, and kill the men who killed his father. Kripa is old. He taught the princes on both sides when they were boys, and he has fought this whole war beside Duryodhana. Now, half awake under a banyan, he has a few minutes to change his nephew's mind.
screen: `KRIPA IS WOKEN.` → `THE PLAN IS SPOKEN.` → `A FEW MINUTES TO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Kripa doesn't shout. In Ganguli's telling he starts with an idea: success needs two things together, what fate gives and what a person does. Effort alone isn't enough, and neither is fate. Then he gets practical. Don't decide this alone, he says, in effect. Let's go to Dhritarashtra, to Gandhari, to the wise Vidura, and ask them what should be done. And he names the thing directly: killing men who are asleep is not honored in this world. Ashvatthama has an answer for everything. The Panchalas broke the rules first, he says. Dhrishtadyumna killed my father while he sat with his weapons laid down. Bhima struck the king below the waist. Why should I keep rules they didn't? He says he cannot sleep while they live. He even says, in effect, that he doesn't care if he's reborn as a worm or an insect for it. Then he yokes his horses and drives off toward the camp. And here is the quiet turn. Kripa and Kritavarma don't go home. They don't warn anyone. They get up and follow him. Kripa gave the right counsel, clearly, kindly, with a better plan, and it wasn't taken. He went along anyway, out of loyalty, or shame, or not wanting his nephew to go alone. The epic doesn't say which. It just shows two good arguments losing to one sleepless man.

852.hook: a gigantic being blocks the gate of the sleeping camp, and every weapon Ashvatthama throws disappears into it

The Pandava camp is dark and quiet. Ashvatthama reaches the gate with Kripa and Kritavarma behind him. And the gate isn't empty. Something is standing there, so large it seems to fill the night. In Ganguli's English it's a being of enormous size, terrible to look at, blazing, wrapped in a tiger skin, with snakes for ornaments and many eyes. It doesn't speak. It just stands between Ashvatthama and the sleeping camp.
screen: `THE CAMP IS ASLEEP.` → `A BEING AT THE GATE.` → `IT DOESN'T SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Ashvatthama does what a warrior does. He attacks. He hurls weapon after weapon at the being, and the being swallows them. Every one vanishes into it, and it stands there untouched. Now he's empty-handed, at night, in front of something he can't fight. And the text lets him think about the advice he ignored. In effect: whoever turns away from the counsel of friends who wish him well comes to grief, and that's what I've done. Then he turns to Mahadeva, the great god, Shiva, and praises him with many names. An altar of gold appears in front of him, with a fire blazing on it, and fierce companions of Shiva crowd around. Ashvatthama offers the only thing he has left. He offers himself, and steps into the fire. Shiva appears, and the text has him speak plainly. He has protected the Panchalas until now, out of regard for Krishna. But their time is over. Then Shiva gives Ashvatthama a sword and enters into his body, and Ashvatthama rises from the fire blazing with that power. It's a hard scene, and the epic doesn't smooth it over. The gate held until a man gave himself up completely. What came through the gate afterward was no longer just Ashvatthama's anger. Shiva's own words say the sleeping camp's time had come.

Dhrishtadyumna is asleep in his tent, on a fine bed, the commander of the Pandava army resting after the war he helped win. He is the man who killed Drona. He wakes because someone is standing on him. It's Ashvatthama, Drona's son. This is the night the whole book is named for, and the epic tells it without looking away. Here it's told more gently, holding on to the few moments the text slows down for: a request, a refusal, and a message brought to a dying king.
screen: `A COMMANDER ASLEEP.` → `DRONA'S SON STANDS OVER HIM.` → `THE NIGHT ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Dhrishtadyumna, pinned down, asks for one thing. In Ganguli's telling he begs Ashvatthama to kill him with a weapon, so that he dies as a warrior and reaches the worlds warriors reach. Ashvatthama refuses. A man who killed his teacher, he says in effect, doesn't deserve a warrior's death. And he kills him without a weapon. Then he moves through the camp. Others wake and fall: Shikhandi, Uttamaujas, Yudhamanyu, and the five young sons of Draupadi, who came to the war with their fathers. In the dark, people wake confused, some striking at each other. Outside, Kripa and Kritavarma stand at the gate and cut down those who flee, and fire is set to the camp. When it's over, the three go back across the field to Duryodhana, still lying where he fell, barely alive. They tell him what they've done. The dying king answers, in effect, that they've done for him what Bhishma, Karna and Drona couldn't, and he dies. But there are names missing from that night. The five Pandava brothers aren't in the camp. Neither are Krishna or Satyaki. Earlier that evening, the text says, Krishna had taken them away to spend the night elsewhere. So the men Ashvatthama most wanted to strike were never there. The ones who died were the commander, the warriors, and Draupadi's sons. That's Sauptika: a vengeance that reaches everyone except its target.

Morning. Dhrishtadyumna's charioteer, one of the few who got away, brings the news to Yudhishthira, and the king falls to the ground. Then Draupadi comes. Her brother is dead. Her five sons are dead. She sits down in front of her husbands and says she'll take no food until Ashvatthama pays for this. And she names what she wants. Ashvatthama was born with a jewel on his head. She wants to see it brought back, and worn by Yudhishthira.
screen: `THE NEWS AT DAWN.` → `DRAUPADI SITS DOWN.` → `SHE ASKS FOR THE JEWEL.`

segments.voice: Bhima rides out at once. Krishna warns the others that Bhima is in danger: Drona once taught his son a weapon called Brahmashira, terrible enough to burn the worlds, and Ashvatthama is reckless enough to use it. So Krishna, Arjuna and Yudhishthira follow. They find Ashvatthama on the bank of the Ganga, sitting among sages with Vyasa. When he sees them, he picks up a blade of grass, charges it as that weapon, and lets it go. Arjuna answers with the same weapon. Two fires rise to meet each other. Then two sages, Narada and Vyasa, step between the weapons to save the world. Arjuna, who has kept his vows, can call his weapon back, and he does. Ashvatthama can't. So he turns his toward the wombs of the Pandava women. Krishna answers that Uttara's child, the unborn son of Abhimanyu, will live, because Krishna himself will revive him. Then Krishna curses Ashvatthama: to wander the earth alone, sick, shunned, for a very long time. Ashvatthama gives up the jewel. They carry it back to Draupadi, and she hands it to Yudhishthira, and he wears it. This week opened in the shadow of a blow on a holy plain, and it closes with a jewel on a king's head: a grieving mother's demand met, and the next generation saved by one promise.
